<1>Who decides what you see in an online store or on a social network?</1>

A friendly screen, kind replies, a caring tone and familiar language are also part of the platform's design. And they can make a loss seem acceptable and a complaint seem like an overreaction before any dispute even begins.

In many cases the conflict is managed before it even exists. The platform does not only look after your initial sign-up, because it also manages how much harm you will put up with and how much energy you still have to react.
In platform-governed ecosystems, conflict does not begin when the user decides to litigate, complain or formalize disagreement.<1>p. 780</1>
What are you consuming besides the service?
You pay for access, content or performance. But you also get an environment that presents itself as clear, helpful, attentive and trustworthy, and that is part of what the platform delivers.

That trust does not arise on its own from good service. It is often produced, adjusted and maintained by the design of the screen and of customer support. That is why the law does not look only at the written contract or at a single clause, and also looks at the way the environment speaks to you.

Trust does not need to come as a formal guarantee to have an effect. It is enough that it leads you to put up with friction, accept vague explanations, treat a loss as normal and keep using the service even after it has gotten worse.
The user does not consume only access, utility, content or performance.<1>p. 781</1>
They consume an environment that presents itself as intelligible, assistive, responsive and, to some extent, worthy of practical credit.<1>p. 781</1>
On platforms, trust is not a spontaneous by-product of the good performance of the service.<1>p. 781</1>
Frequently, it is produced, calibrated and maintained by design.<1>p. 781</1>
This trust need not take the solemn form of an express guarantee to produce relevant legal effects.<1>p. 781</1>

It is enough that it acts steadily on the ordinary interpretation of the experience and on the user's willingness to bear friction, accept vague justifications, normalize losses and remain in the cycle of use even when enjoyment has already been functionally degraded.<1>p. 781</1>
How does a complaint get erased?
<1>The loss becomes routine.</1> In a service you use every day, small frustrations get absorbed and stop looking like a problem. They start to look like the system working normally.

<1>The friction gets another name.</1> What could be read as a failure or an abuse shows up as a technical adjustment, a temporary limitation, a security measure, a necessary update or just a step in using the service.

<1>Support listens but does not solve anything.</1> Friendly messages, replies that seem to explain and support channels built to receive the complaint without getting to the bottom of the problem slowly drain your strength to push back.
The conflict does not go away. It is just governed before it turns into a formal complaint or a lawsuit, and so the loss becomes tolerable noise.
The loss ceases to appear as an exceptional event and comes to be metabolized as part of the normal functioning of the system.<1>p. 781</1>

Instead of promptly triggering a reading of inadequacy or abusiveness, it can be reframed by the platform as a technical adjustment, temporary limitation, understandable inconvenience, security measure, necessary update or simple step of use.<1>p. 781</1>

Persona, operational cordiality, messages of closeness, excessively reassuring simplifications, explanatory-looking replies and support circuits designed to absorb disagreement without actually reconstructing the problem can operate, together, as a technique of demobilization.<1>p. 782</1>
The conflict does not disappear.<1>p. 782</1>
It is governed in its pre-legal phase, through mechanisms that turn loss into tolerable noise, opacity into normality and asymmetry into an absorbable experience.<1>p. 782</1>
Is every bit of company friendliness a problem?
No. Accessible language, polite support and the effort to keep a good relationship with you are legitimate. What matters is not whether you felt more or less welcome.

The problem begins when friendliness starts to serve, in a structural way, to neutralize the complaint. For example, when the platform gives a sense of transparency without really explaining, gives the impression of listening without opening a real way to challenge, or uses a human tone without taking on the duty to justify what it did.

<1>Semiotic vulnerability.</1> It is the disadvantage of someone who has to rely on signs that someone else controls. Here it grows, because trust itself is used to lower your resistance. The platform produces enough signs of clarity and care for you to settle in, even when what you use has already been harmed.
The central vulnerability of this subtype is, once again, semiotic vulnerability, but now intensified by the management of trust as a way of modulating resistance.<1>p. 782</1>
The user faces an ecosystem that produces enough signs of intelligibility and care to induce accommodation, even when the materiality of enjoyment has already been compromised.<1>p. 782</1>
And what if the rumor about the next skin decides what you buy?

In games, rumors, leaks and unofficial previews of skins, champions and events circulate all the time. People who make a living leaking information, influencers and specialized channels piece together partial images and assumed calendars and turn it all into a story that feels like a promise.

So you wait, put off purchases, save money and rearrange what you want based on signs nobody has confirmed. You buy with the awaited skin in mind, and not only what is on sale. The future starts to organize the present of your spending.
While nothing is official, the company can deny, change the calendar, alter the product or just watch the reaction. It reaps the engagement without owning up to what was announced ahead of time.

This does not mean every rumor is the company's fault, or that it controls everything the community says. No one can demand that it stop every leak or confirm every rumor. The point is a different one. Once a specific, repeated expectation capable of guiding your spending has taken hold, the company is no longer in a neutral position.
The rumor, in this context, does not remain mere noise external to the supply.<1>p. 784</1>

One does not buy only the available object. One also buys in light of the anticipated object, the sensed event, the awaited skin, the imagined update. The future comes to organize the present of consumption.<1>p. 785</1>

When content circulates without official confirmation, the platform preserves a margin of plausible deniability and strategic flexibility to reshape schedules, alter products, recalibrate offers or simply harvest reactions without fully owning, as communication, what was anticipated.<1>p. 784</1>

This is not about imposing an impracticable duty to prevent every rumor, every leak or every community speculation. Nor is it about turning the company into a universal certifier of rumors.<1>p. 786</1>

It lies in recognizing that, once a specific, reiterated expectation materially capable of guiding consumption decisions has settled into the ecosystem, the platform no longer remains in a neutral position.<1>p. 785</1>
This also has a name

<1>Hypercuratorial anticipation.</1> It is the way the platform governs what you expect from the game's future. It does not act only through announcements, trailers and seasons. It can also act through rumors organized by third parties, which the company tolerates because they keep the community watching and ready to spend.
Hypercuratorial anticipation, already delimited as a mechanism governing the present and the future of enjoyment, takes on a specific form here.<1>p. 784</1>

It can also operate through unofficial circuits of curated rumor, in which partial images, technical references, fragmentary leaks, assumed calendars and speculation deemed plausible are organized by leakers, influencers and channels specialized in narratives of a consumable future.<1>p. 784</1>
Which rumor situations weigh the most?
<1>Silence in the face of an expectation that already moves the community.</1> The company stays quiet or answers evasively about something that is already guiding how players plan.

<1>The denial that later falls apart.</1> The company denies something specific and then does practically the same thing. That contradiction between what it said and what it did may weigh when the question is whether there was deception.
<1>The expectation confirmed and then let down.</1> The company confirms or feeds the expectation and then does not deliver, without a proportionate explanation.
In none of these cases is the problem that the service changes, because change is part of it. The problem is using that freedom to never have to explain anything.
In this scenario, the contradiction between communication and conduct may acquire its own weight for examining deceptiveness and legitimately formed trust.<1>p. 786</1>

In all these situations, the point is not to punish the mutability inherent in continuous digital services, but to prevent their structural flexibility from being turned into communicational immunity.<1>p. 786</1>
Here the evidence runs through the way the platform talks to you. What counts is reconstructing the path that made your frustration disappear.
The language on the screen and in the messages.
The path through customer support, step by step.
The canned replies and explanations you received.
The way the loss was presented to you.
The steps that led you to accept, wait, play it down or give up.
With rumors, also keep what was circulating, when it was circulating, what you asked the company and what it answered or failed to answer. Screenshots and dates help a lot.
<1>Thinking only the contract counts.</1> The way the company talks to you also has effects, and not just the clauses and formal acts.
<1>Thinking trust is just your own feeling.</1> Trust, here, is something the environment organizes, and not a private impression.
<1>Thinking the conflict only begins when you complain outside the platform.</1> The platform may govern precisely the moment when you realize you lost something.
The first is the tendency to consider the discursive dimension of supply irrelevant, as if only clauses and formal acts produced legal effects.<1>p. 783</1>
The second is the tendency to treat trust as a private feeling of the user, and not as a functional arrangement of the environment.<1>p. 783</1>
Customer support must actually resolve things, and not just absorb the complaint. The company must explain in a way you can understand and check, and must justify the decisions that affect you.

When rumors are already driving players' spending, the company does not need to confirm every speculation. But when it is asked directly, or when the rumor settles in persistently, there may be a duty to clarify, not to contradict itself and to justify. In that setting, staying silent may stop being a neutral choice and become a lack of relevant information.

[...] a duty of clarification, non-contradiction and justification when ecosystemically relevant rumors, endowed with sufficient social credibility and functionally capable of influencing spending plans, purchase priorities or the wait for enjoyment, are the object of specific prompting by users or become persistently part of the consumption environment.<1>p. 786</1>
Omission, in this setting, ceases to be a simple neutral communicational choice and may become relevant informational insufficiency in a context of operative expectation.<1>p. 786</1>

The path usually goes beyond asking for compensation for what already happened. It may be possible to demand that customer support be fixed, that explanations become clear and that there be ways to challenge that lead somewhere, and not just to a place where the complaint vanishes.
In the most serious cases, when erasing challenges is part of how the platform normally works, the very purpose of the design may come into question.
The legal response compatible with this setting tends to require more than mere retrospective reparation.<1>p. 783</1>
Did you lose something and get convinced it was normal, temporary or necessary?
Was customer support kind but never really explained or solved anything?
Was there no clear way to challenge the decision?
